Next, 6.2.2 proposed amendments to CO3-027 borrowing for capital projects. Mr. Hack.
Thank you, Mr. Chair. This report is recommending amendments to the borrowing for capital projects, council policy, specifically on how public notices provided.
Currently public notices provided immediately after the approval of a budget that has boring as a funding source identified regardless of whether the boring is provided internally or externally.

While this public notice addresses the requirement in the bylaw, it lacks key boring details such as boring method, timing, term, interest rate and repayment requirements as actual boring may not occur for several months or years into the future.

As such, the recommended amendments include moving the public notice requirement closer to the time of actual boring, which would include these key details, and to not requiring public notice for projects that utilize internal boring as those are not bored from a third party or impact the city's external debt obligations.

It's important to note that even with these changes all capital projects must still receive council approval through the budget process or a post budget report, which would identify boring as a source of funding as well.
As well as an authorization to borrow report when the time of borrowing comes.

Information reports. Six point three point one implications to neighborhood land development fund allocation policy changes.
Thank you, Mr. Chair. This report provides information in response to SPC finances direction from February 4th, 2026.
To report back on the potential impact of amending the neighborhood land development fund allocation policy to increase the allocation to affordable housing from 15% to 25%.
As outlined in the report, increasing the affordable housing allocation from 15 to 25% would help strengthen the city's ability to contribute to affordable housing projects.
Respond to emerging housing pressures and potentially leverage other governing funding government funding opportunities.
On the other side, a 10% increase in affordable housing reserve would require a 10% decrease to the contribution to the property realises reserve or discretionary use purposes.

Reactions to the discretionary use would reduce the amount of funding that has historically been utilized for projects such as the construction of chief Mr. Wasis Bridge and the traffic bridge project.
The East, Leisure Center and various roadway and recreation projects.
Less funding from this source means that projects such as these will be more difficult to fund in the future requiring more property tax contributions or less projects overall.
So the property realized reserved allocation would impact the city's ability to buy land for future development or civic projects.

It is important to note that within the report it identifies that maintaining the current 15% allocation to the affordable housing reserve does not necessarily mean that additional funding could not be allocated in the future when dividends are declared as part of the discretionary portion of this funding formula.
